description: Muslim teaching on contraception, divorce, gender equality and discrimination in the family.
content_html:
Contraception and Family Planning

Muslims hold divergent views on contraception, but the classical starting point is a set of hadith reports that companions of the Prophet practised ‘azl (withdrawal) during his lifetime and he did not forbid it. These reports, found in Sahih al-Bukhari 34:432 and 62:136, are the main evidence used to permit family planning, provided both spouses agree to it. ‘azl is not something one spouse can impose on the other — mutual consent is the key condition.

Mainstream Sunni and Shi’a scholars extend this reasoning to modern reversible methods, such as the pill or condom, since the underlying principle — spacing pregnancies for the health of the mother and the stability of the family — is the same. Permanent sterilisation and abortion are treated far more restrictively. Sterilisation is permitted by only some scholars, and usually only for clear medical necessity, because it removes the possibility of future children altogether. Abortion as a method of contraception is not accepted; most scholars apply especially strict conditions once the pregnancy has passed the point of ensoulment, allowing termination only where the mother’s life is at risk.

Key Fact

Sahih al-Bukhari 34:432 and 62:136 report that companions practised ‘azl (withdrawal) during the Prophet’s lifetime without him forbidding it. Mainstream Sunni and Shi’a scholars use this as the classical basis for permitting reversible contraception, on condition that both spouses agree.

Non-religious Humanists generally see family planning as a matter of personal autonomy and responsible parenthood, judging each case by its likely consequences for the family's wellbeing rather than by a fixed rule. A similar case-by-case approach is found in situation ethics — a Christian ethical theory developed by Joseph Fletcher, which judges the right action by whichever choice is the most loving in the situation. Muslim responses often agree that protecting the wellbeing of the family supports responsible family planning, but insist this remains a private decision for the couple within marriage, guided by the Qur'an and hadith rather than by a purely case-by-case ethic.

A minority of more conservative scholars argue that deliberately limiting family size can sit uneasily with tawakkul — trust that Allah will provide for the children he grants — and with the duty to grow the ummah. On this view, contraception should be occasional rather than a permanent rejection of children. Mainstream scholarship responds that trusting Allah is entirely compatible with sensible planning, in the same way that working for a living does not contradict trust in Allah’s provision.

Divorce and Remarriage

Islam permits divorce (talaq) but treats it as strongly discouraged, to be used only once a marriage genuinely cannot be saved. A husband-pronounced talaq is followed by a waiting period set out in Surah 2:226–241. During this ‘iddah, the couple typically continues living under the same roof, the husband continues to provide financial support, and reconciliation is actively encouraged. Muslims believe family arbiters from both sides should be tried before any divorce is finalised.

A wife who wishes to end her marriage may seek khul’, in which she typically returns her mahr (the gift given to her at marriage) in exchange for release. Both talaq and khul’ allow remarriage once any ‘iddah has been completed — but not during the waiting period itself.

Key Fact

Surah 2:226–241 sets out the ‘iddah waiting period following talaq. Reconciliation is encouraged and financial support continues throughout it; only once the wife's ‘iddah is complete is she free to remarry, and the divorce becomes final.

Sunni and Shi’a law differ on how a valid divorce is performed. Shi’a jurisprudence requires talaq to be pronounced in Arabic, before two just male witnesses, in a single sitting, and does not recognise a triple pronouncement made all at once as ending the marriage outright. Several Sunni schools of law have historically treated a triple pronouncement made in one sitting as immediately and irrevocably binding, though this remains debated, and some modern Muslim-majority states have introduced reforms restricting the practice.

Non-religious Humanists generally view divorce as a personal decision, best judged by whichever outcome causes the least harm and greatest wellbeing for those involved — an approach consistent with situation ethics. Muslim responses point out that Islam already discourages divorce and requires attempts at reconciliation and arbitration first, so the two positions often reach similar practical outcomes even though they start from different foundations.

Equality of Men and Women in the Family

Surah 4 sets out rights and responsibilities within marriage. A husband must pay his wife a mahr at the time of marriage, and it remains hers alone. A wife keeps her own name, her own earnings, and the right to own and manage property independently of her husband. Muslim teaching presents these as protections that give women financial security within marriage.

Muslims hold divergent views on how far men’s and women’s roles should differ. A complementarian reading understands qiwamah — a husband’s duty to maintain and protect his wife — as a form of headship, with distinct but equally valued roles for men and women. An egalitarian, more reformist reading understands qiwamah as a financial responsibility only, arguing that spouses should reach decisions together through mutual consultation as equal partners.

Muslims point to the time of Muhammad as evidence that Islam improved women’s position compared with earlier custom. Khadijah, the Prophet’s first wife, was an independent and successful merchant who employed Muhammad before their marriage. Revelation at this time gave women the right to inherit, the right to consent to their own marriage, and the right to own property — rights that were not reliably guaranteed to women under the customs that came before.

Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

Surah 33:35 addresses believing men and believing women together, in matching terms, listing the same qualities of devotion, honesty, patience and charity in men and women alike, and promising both the same reward from Allah. Muslims regard this as clear evidence that men and women are of equal worth and standing before Allah, even where their social roles may differ.

Key Fact

Surah 33:35 lists identical qualities of faith for believing men and believing women and promises them the same reward from Allah — a foundation text for Muslim teaching that gender prejudice and discrimination are wrong.

Muslims point to examples of gender equality in action: women have historically served as respected scholars and narrators of hadith, and today many Muslim women lead charities, teach in mosques and Islamic schools, and hold professional and academic positions. Practice still varies between communities — mosques differ in how they arrange space for men and women, and Muslims hold divergent views on whether women should lead mixed congregational prayer or serve as imams, with reformist voices arguing for greater inclusion and traditionalist scholars maintaining established separate roles.
exam_tip_html: Watch the command word. “Outline three” wants three separate, distinct points — not one point explained three times. For the 5-mark “Explain two with sources” question, you must name a source of authority (a surah, hadith collection, or named Islamic concept) and apply it, not just state a belief in general terms. On the 12-mark evaluation, include a non-religious viewpoint as well as divergent Muslim views (Sunni and Shi’a, or traditionalist and reformist): the Evaluate command word asks you to consider different points of view and build logical chains of reasoning to a justified conclusion, so showing that Muslims disagree gives you more to appraise.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Contraception is permitted by mainstream scholars on the basis of hadith reports of ‘azl, with mutual consent required; sterilisation and abortion are treated far more restrictively.
  • Divorce is permitted but discouraged; Sunni and Shi’a law differ on how talaq must be performed, and khul’ gives wives a route to end a marriage.
  • Surah 4 and Surah 33:35 are used to support both complementarian and egalitarian readings of gender roles, and to reject gender prejudice and discrimination.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why some Muslims believe contraception is permissible within marriage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three distinct points: hadith evidence that companions practised 'azl without the Prophet forbidding it (1); the requirement of mutual spousal consent (1); protecting the wellbeing (maslahah) of the family, such as spacing pregnancies for the mother's health (1). Other valid reasons accepted.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Sunni and Shi'a Muslims differ in their approach to performing a divorce.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three distinct points: Shi'a law requires the pronouncement to be made in Arabic (1); before two just male witnesses (1); in a single sitting, and does not recognise a triple pronouncement in one sitting as immediately ending the marriage, unlike the historical position of several Sunni schools (1). Other valid points accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim teachings about the equality of men and women in marriage.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for each of two developed points (2+2). Point 1: a complementarian reading of qiwamah gives the husband a duty of maintenance and protection (1), understood by some as a form of headship with distinct but equally valued roles (1). Point 2: a wife's right to keep her mahr and manage her own property shows financial independence within marriage (1), supporting an egalitarian reading in which decisions are reached through mutual consultation (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim teachings about gender prejudice and discrimination, referring to a source of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks. Point 1: Surah 33:35 addresses believing men and believing women in identical terms (1), promising them equal reward regardless of gender (1). Point 2: Muslims oppose discrimination through women's roles as scholars, teachers and community leaders today (1), shown by examples such as women leading charities or teaching in mosques (1). Named source of authority (Surah 33:35) correctly referenced and applied (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim teachings about contraception, referring to a source of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks. Point 1: hadith reports that companions practised 'azl without the Prophet forbidding it (1), used as the basis for permitting modern reversible methods (1). Point 2: a minority view holds that family planning may conflict with tawakkul (1), meaning contraception should never be a permanent rejection of children (1). Named source of authority (Sahih al-Bukhari 34:432 or 62:136) correctly referenced and applied (1).

practice_questions.text: 'A Muslim couple should always try family arbitration before seeking a divorce.' Evaluate this statement, considering Muslim and non-religious viewpoints. In your answer you should refer to a range of arguments, reach a justified conclusion and refer to religious teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Top band (10-12): Sustained, balanced reasoning covering Muslim teaching (talaq as strongly discouraged, the 'iddah period as space for reconciliation, the tradition of family arbiters) and non-religious or situation ethics perspectives (arbitration may not always be needed if the most loving outcome is a swift, clean separation), leading to a clear, justified conclusion. Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear reasoning with developed points on both sides and relevant sources, conclusion follows from the discussion but may be less fully developed. Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant points made with limited development; may be one-sided or make limited reference to sources. Low band (1-3): Basic or list-like points with little development or reasoned argument.

right: Withdrawal, the classical hadith basis for permitting contraception
A gift given by a husband to his wife at marriage, which remains hers alone
A husband's duty of maintenance and protection, read differently by complementarian and egalitarian Muslims
The Prophet's first wife, an independent and successful merchant

glossary_terms.definition: Withdrawal (coitus interruptus), reported in hadith as practised by companions of the Prophet without prohibition, used as the classical basis for permitting contraception in Islam.
Trust in Allah's provision and plan, cited by some conservative scholars as a reason to be cautious about deliberate family planning.
The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or widowhood, during which remarriage is not permitted and reconciliation is encouraged.
A wife-initiated form of divorce in which she typically returns her mahr in exchange for release from the marriage.
A mandatory gift of money or property given by a husband to his wife at marriage, which remains her own property.
The Qur'an's concept of a husband's maintenance and protective responsibility toward his wife, read by some as headship and by others as a financial duty only.

A Christian ethical theory developed by Joseph Fletcher in the 1960s, which rejects fixed rules and judges the right action by whichever choice is the most loving (agape) in a particular situation; its case-by-case reasoning is sometimes compared with non-religious approaches to family issues.
